TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER FINAL-WAGE TIMING (LABOR CODE § 201.3) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Staffing, Inc.

TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER FINAL-WAGE TIMING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
California Labor Code section 201.3 sets a distinct set of wage-timing rules for an employee of a "temporary services employer" who is assigned to work for that employer's client — rules that operate differently from, and in some circumstances alongside, the general immediate-on-discharge and 72-hour-on-quit deadlines in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme Staffing, Inc., recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.3's own rules, described in the information that follows, turn on whether Acme Staffing, Inc. meets the statute's own multi-part definition of a "temporary services employer" and whether Jordan Lee was assigned to work for one of that employer's clients. Naming Jordan Lee and Acme Staffing, Inc. here does not itself determine that Acme Staffing, Inc. is a temporary services employer within the meaning of Section 201.3, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular working relationship.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER"
Labor Code section 201.3 defines a "temporary services employer," for purposes of that section's own timing rules, as an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers to perform services for them, and that itself performs all seven of a listed set of functions: negotiating with clients and customers over matters such as when and where services are provided, the type of work, working conditions, and price; determining worker assignments or reassignments, even if a worker may refuse a specific assignment; retaining authority to reassign a worker a client has found unacceptable; actually assigning or reassigning workers to clients; setting workers' rate of pay; paying workers from its own account; and retaining the right to hire and terminate workers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "“Temporary services employer” means an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers to perform services for the clients or customers and that performs all of the following functions:(A) Negotiates with clients and customers for matters such as the time and place where the services are to be provided, the type of work, the working conditions, and the quality and price of the services.(B) Determines assignments or reassignments of workers, even if workers retain the right to refuse specific assignments.(C) Retains the authority to assign or reassign a worker to another client or customer when the worker is determined unacceptable by a specific client or customer.(D) Assigns or reassigns workers to perform services for clients or customers.(E) Sets the rate of pay of workers, whether or not through negotiation.(F) Pays workers from its own account or accounts.(G) Retains the right to hire and terminate workers."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — statutory definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivision (a)(1)), used as real evidence of the specific seven-function test this statute itself uses to define a "temporary services employer" — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular business does or does not meet this definition. The statute requires an employing unit to perform all seven listed functions, not merely some of them, to fall within this definition; this clause does not resolve whether any particular staffing arrangement in fact satisfies every element. This document addresses only this section's own definition for purposes of Section 201.3's wage-timing rules; it does not address the separate common-law or other statutory tests (such as joint-employer or worker-classification standards) that may apply the term "temporary services employer" or a similar label differently for other purposes.

STATUTORY EXCLUSIONS FROM "TEMPORARY SERVICES EMPLOYER," AND RELATED DEFINITIONS
The statute's own definition of "temporary services employer" expressly excludes three categories: a bona fide nonprofit organization that provides temporary service employees to clients, a farm labor contractor as separately defined in Labor Code section 1682(b), and a garment manufacturing employer, which for this section's purposes carries the same meaning as "contractor" under Labor Code section 2671(d). The statute also defines two related terms it uses throughout the rest of the section: an "employing unit" carries the same meaning given that term in Unemployment Insurance Code section 135, and "client" and "customer" mean the person with whom a temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more of the temporary services employer's own employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(2) “Temporary services employer” does not include any of the following:(A) A bona fide nonprofit organization that provides temporary service employees to clients.(B) A farm labor contractor, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1682.(C) A garment manufacturing employer, which, for purposes of this section, has the same meaning as “contractor,” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 2671.(3) “Employing unit” has the same meaning as defined in Section 135 of the Unemployment Insurance Code.(4) “Client” and “customer” mean the person with whom a temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more individuals employed by the temporary services employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(2)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — exclusions and related definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (a)(2), (a)(3), and (a)(4)), used as real evidence of this section's own exclusions and cross-referenced definitions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular organization falls within or outside one of these three excluded categories. This clause does not independently fetch or quote the cross-referenced definitions in Labor Code section 1682(b) (farm labor contractor), Labor Code section 2671(d) (garment manufacturing "contractor"), or Unemployment Insurance Code section 135 (employing unit); it states only that Section 201.3 itself points to those other sections, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. The three exclusions and the two related definitions are all part of the same statutory subdivision structure (paragraphs (2) through (4) of subdivision (a)) and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources.

THE GENERAL RULE: WAGES DUE NO LESS OFTEN THAN WEEKLY, REGARDLESS OF WHEN THE ASSIGNMENT ENDS
Unlike the general rule that final wages are due only when employment actually ends, Labor Code section 201.3 requires a temporary services employer to pay an employee assigned to a client no less frequently than weekly throughout the assignment, regardless of when that assignment ends — wages for work performed in a given calendar week are due by the regular payday of the following calendar week, and a temporary services employer that pays on this schedule is deemed to have timely paid wages upon completion of the assignment. The statute sets a parallel, weekly-based rule for a narrower category of workers: an employee of a temporary services employer in the security services industry who is a registered security guard employed by a licensed private patrol operator and assigned to a client is due wages no less frequently than weekly as well, but measured by "workweek" as that term is separately defined in Labor Code section 500, rather than by calendar week.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any calendar week shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following calendar week. A temporary services employer shall be deemed to have timely paid wages upon completion of an assignment if wages are paid in compliance with this subdivision.(B) Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer in the security services industry is a security guard who is registered pursuant to Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, is employed by a private patrol operator licensed pursuant to that chapter, and is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any workweek, as defined under Section 500, shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following workweek."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(1)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — weekly payday requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(1)(A) and (b)(1)(B)), used as real evidence of this section's own baseline weekly-payday rule and its security-guard variant — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular worker is or is not a registered security guard employed by a licensed private patrol operator within the meaning of Business and Professions Code Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580), which this clause does not independently fetch or quote. Both rules are expressly made subject to the more specific rules in paragraphs (2) through (5) of the same subdivision, addressed in separate clauses of this document; this clause states only the general weekly baseline, not those exceptions. This clause also does not independently fetch or quote Labor Code section 500's definition of "workweek," relying only on Section 201.3's own cross-reference to it.

TWO SITUATIONS REQUIRING PAYMENT AT THE END OF EACH DAY
Two categories of temporary-services assignments carry a faster, daily payment rule instead of the general weekly rule. First, if an employee is assigned to a client on a day-to-day basis, wages for that day are due at the end of the day, regardless of when the assignment ends, provided the employee reports to or assembles at the temporary services employer's office or another location, is dispatched to the client's worksite each day and returns or reports back upon completing the assignment, and the employee's work is not executive, administrative, professional, or clerical, as the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders define those terms. Second, and independent of the day-to-day condition, if an employee is assigned to work for a client that is engaged in a trade dispute, wages are due at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(2) If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends, if each of the following occurs:(A) The employee reports to or assembles at the office of the temporary services employer or other location.(B) The employee is dispatched to a client’s worksite each day and returns to or reports to the office of the temporary services employer or other location upon completion of the assignment.(C) The employee’s work is not executive, administrative, or professional, as defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical.(3) If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client engaged in a trade dispute, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — daily-pay rules for day-to-day and trade-dispute assignments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(2) and (b)(3)), used as real evidence of this section's own two daily-pay triggers — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment in fact meets the day-to-day criteria or involves a client "engaged in a trade dispute," a term this clause does not independently define. This clause does not independently fetch or quote the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders' own definitions of "executive," "administrative," or "professional" work, relying only on Section 201.3's own cross-reference to those wage orders. Both subdivisions are part of the same statutory paragraph structure and are treated here as one source describing two related exceptions, not as independent corroborating sources.

DISCHARGE AND QUIT FALL BACK TO THE GENERAL SECTIONS 201 AND 202 RULES
Section 201.3 states its own exception to the weekly and daily rules described elsewhere in this document for the two events that end an assignment outright: if the employee is discharged by the temporary services employer (or a "leasing employer"), wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 201 — the general rule that wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due immediately. If the employee instead quits their employment with the temporary services employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 202 — the general rule that wages are due within 72 hours of quitting, or immediately if the employee gave at least 72 hours' notice of the intent to quit. In other words, once an assignment ends through a discharge or a quit rather than continuing, Section 201.3's own weekly or daily timing rules stop controlling and the same immediate or 72-hour deadlines that apply to employees generally take over.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(4) If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and is discharged by the temporary services employer or leasing employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 201.(5) If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and quits his or her employment with the temporary services employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 202."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(4)-(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — discharge and quit revert to Sections 201 and 202 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, general immediate-payment-on-discharge rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.)
  "If an employee not having a written contract for a definite period quits his or her employment, his or her wages shall become due and payable not later than 72 hours thereafter, unless the employee has given 72 hours previous notice of his or her intention to quit, in which case the employee is entitled to his or her wages at the time of quitting."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 202(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, general 72-hour rule for an employee who quits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=202.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(4) and (b)(5), together with the first sentences of Labor Code sections 201(a) and 202(a)), used as real evidence that a discharge or a quit ends the special weekly/daily timing rules and reverts to the general discharge and quit rules — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular separation in this or any specific case was in fact a "discharge" or a "quit" within the meaning of these statutes. This clause does not restate the remainder of Sections 201 and 202 (including the state-employer leave-deferral provisions in their later subdivisions, which do not concern temporary services employees), and does not restate the mailing options each section separately provides, both addressed only as background here. Section 201.3 does not itself define "leasing employer," a term this subdivision (b)(4) uses without further elaboration; this clause does not resolve what falls within that term.

THE WEEKLY/DAILY RULES STOP APPLYING AFTER 90 CONSECUTIVE DAYS ON ONE ASSIGNMENT, UNLESS THE EMPLOYER ALREADY PAYS WEEKLY
Section 201.3 places its own outer limit on how long its special timing rules continue to apply to a single ongoing assignment. If an employee is assigned to work for the same client for more than 90 consecutive calendar days, the section stops applying to that assignment at all — unless the temporary services employer already pays the employee weekly in compliance with the general weekly-payday rule described elsewhere in this document. Where the section stops applying, this document's other clauses describing Section 201.3's own weekly, daily, and discharge/quit timing rules no longer govern that particular assignment by their own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(6) If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client for over 90 consecutive calendar days, this section does not apply unless the temporary services employer pays the employee weekly in compliance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(6) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — 90-consecutive-day limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivision (b)(6)), used as real evidence of this section's own 90-consecutive-day limitation — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment did or did not last more than 90 consecutive calendar days, or that any particular temporary services employer was or was not already paying weekly at that point. The statute does not itself state which other wage-timing rule then governs an assignment once Section 201.3 stops applying to it; this clause does not resolve that question, an honest gap disclosed rather than answered by assumption — the general final-wage-timing and regular-payday rules addressed elsewhere in this corpus may be relevant, but this clause does not determine that they, specifically, replace Section 201.3 for any given assignment.

VIOLATIONS TRIGGER THE SECTION 203 WAITING-TIME PENALTY; THE SECTION DOES NOT LIMIT OTHER RIGHTS
Section 201.3 does not create its own freestanding penalty amount. Instead, it states that a temporary services employer who violates the section is subject to the civil penalties Labor Code section 203 provides, in addition to any other penalties otherwise available at law, and that nothing in Section 201.3 is to be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available under state or federal law. Section 203 itself expressly lists Section 201.3 among the final-wage statutes whose willful, unabated violation triggers the general waiting-time penalty: continuation of the employee's wages, as a penalty, from the due date at the same rate the employee was earning until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days, with an exception where the employee avoids or refuses tender of payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(c) A temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided for in Section 203 and to any other penalties available at law.(d) This section shall not be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available under state or federal law."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, temporary services employer — penalty cross-reference and savings clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.3.)
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days. An employee who secretes or absents themselves to avoid payment to them, or who refuses to receive the payment when fully tendered to them, including any penalty then accrued under this section, is not entitled to any benefit under this section for the time during which the employee so avoids payment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, general waiting-time penalty for willful nonpayment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (c) and (d), together with Labor Code § 203(a)), used as real evidence that a Section 201.3 violation is penalized under the general Section 203 waiting-time framework and that Section 201.3 does not itself displace other rights — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular late or short payment by any particular temporary services employer was "willful" within the meaning of Section 203, which is a separate legal standard this clause does not analyze here. This clause does not restate the full mechanics of the Section 203 penalty (including its 30-day cap arithmetic or its own statute-of-limitations provision in subdivision (b)) beyond what is quoted below; this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses those general mechanics in more depth. This clause does not identify what "other penalties available at law" beyond Section 203 might apply to a Section 201.3 violation, an honest gap the statute's own text leaves open rather than one this clause resolves.
